On Ostrek-4, a tidally locked super-Earth circling a dim red dwarf, there is no true day or night—only a narrow twilight band between a scorching permanent day-side and a frozen night-side. In that band, among forests of silica-rich “chimney trees” growing around geothermal vents, lives the veil-walker.

It is about the size of a small pony but built low and long, like a fusion of a centipede, a pangolin, and a cuttlefish. Its body is divided into eleven overlapping armored segments. At a distance the plates look matte black, but when the red dwarf’s light strikes them they shimmer with copper-green and deep violet. Beneath the armor, the skin is rubbery and moist, threaded with bioluminescent canals that pulse slow amber when the creature is calm and rapid blue-white when it is alarmed.

Instead of a head, it has a front sensory rosette: a bulbous cluster of five eyes. Two are large and forward-facing; three are smaller, set above and to the sides. The eyes have vertical pupils and a reflective layer that lets them see in near-infrared, useful in the perpetual dusk. Around them, a fringe of feathery tendrils constantly tastes the air. Its mouth is not a jaw but a retractable proboscis ringed with six grinding plates. With it, the veil-walker can rasp lichen from stone, crack open carrion bones, or inject digestive enzymes into prey and drink the softened tissue.

It walks on six limbs. The four rear legs are stout and clawed, ending in adhesive pads. The two forelimbs are longer and more delicate, ending in fan-shaped membranes that flare like sails. These fans are used in courtship, in threat displays, and to shed heat when the creature wanders too close to the hot edge of the day-side. Along its spine runs a row of hollow quills. When wind passes through them, they produce a low, haunting whistle; the veil-walker can also vibrate them to send infrasound through the ground. Its tail ends in a glowing lure, a sac of symbiotic bacteria used to attract small burrowing prey and signal others of its kind.

Its blood is pale blue and copper-based, pumped by three hearts: two small gill-hearts and one central heart. It breathes through spiracles along its flanks and two bellows-like lungs on its back. It is an omnivorous scavenger and grazer, feeding on silica lichens, geothermal moss, carrion, and small invertebrates. It can go weeks without food by entering a torpor in which its body temperature drops and its glow fades to a faint ember.

Veil-walkers are solitary and territorial but rarely aggressive unless provoked. They communicate through ground vibrations, bioluminescent patterns, and chemical trails left by glands in their feet. They are curious and have been observed using stones to crack hard-shelled eggs and resin to plug wounds. During solar storms, they secrete a waxy cocoon and enter a state called “glass sleep” for days. They also form a mutualistic bond with sparkflies, tiny flying scavengers that clean their plates; the veil-walker tolerates them and protects their nests.

Mating occurs once every seven years, when the terminator shifts with the planet’s slow seasons. Two adults exchange gametes through their proboscises, and the larger parent later lays a clutch of gelatinous eggs in geothermal pools. The larvae are aquatic, translucent, and filter-feed with twelve feathery limbs. After three years, they crawl onto land, shed their larval gills, and begin life as miniature veil-walkers. They mature in twelve years and can live eighty to a hundred. They regenerate lost limbs slowly, and old individuals often bear scars from shadow-kites, their main predators, which hunt by dropping silently out of the dark side.

To a human, the veil-walker would look both beautiful and unsettling: a low, armored, many-eyed creature glowing softly in the dusk, whistling through its spine as it walks. It is a creature of the twilight, perfectly adapted to a world where day and night never truly end.

On Aethe-3, a tidally locked world circling an orange dwarf star, life clings to the narrow twilight band between the sun-scorched day side and the frozen night side. In the warm, shallow wetlands of that band lives a creature human surveyors call the **gloamwalker**. To the native biosphere, it is simply *thurm*—the one who steps in the mud and sings through the ground.

A gloamwalker is roughly the size of a small pony: about 1.4 meters tall at the shoulder and 3 meters from snout to tail. Its body is long, low, and teardrop-shaped, carried on six limbs. The middle four are sturdy walking legs, each ending in three broad toes with retractable claws for gripping slick mud and roots. The front pair are shorter, more delicate grasping arms, with four fingers and two opposable digits, used to dig, tear food, and manipulate objects. The tail is flattened and muscular, used as a rudder when swimming and as a drum when communicating.

Its hide is covered in overlapping plates of tough, keratin-like chitin. The dorsal plates are semi-translucent and threaded with symbiotic algae, giving the creature a faint emerald glow in the dim light. When warm and healthy, the glow is steady; when frightened or ill, the light stutters and shifts toward violet. Beneath the plates, its skin is leathery and moist, secreting an antimicrobial wax that keeps it from drying out during the long twilight.

The gloamwalker has no true eyes. Instead, a crown of six black sensory stalks rises from its head, each tipped with a lensless pit that detects polarized light, shadow, and movement. Along its snout are electroreceptors that can feel the tiny electrical fields of buried prey. Its hearing is also unusual: it senses low-frequency vibrations through its feet and tail, reading footsteps, water currents, and the rumble of distant geothermal vents. When it vocalizes, it produces clicks and deep pulses that travel through the ground rather than the air.

Its mouth is a vertical slit lined with grinding plates and a muscular, rasping tongue. Two retractable proboscises can dart out to capture small mud-dwelling worms, insect-like skitterers, and mineral-rich algae. The gloamwalker is an omnivorous scavenger and grazer. It uses its grasping arms to pry up silica-rooted plants, then swallows the tough fibers and lets a stone-filled gizzard grind them down. The mist is not deadly, but it burns the eyes and sensory pits of predators. If cornered, it can strike with its heavy tail or retreat into the water, where it swims with serpentine grace.

As a species, the gloamwalker is a keystone of the twilight wetlands. It aerates the mud, spreads spores and seeds, and provides food for larger nocturnal flyers and amphibious predators. Its mouth is a vertical slit flanked by four mandibles. Inside, a rasping tongue scrapes lichen, spores, and flesh from surfaces. Along its spine rises a thin dorsal sail, supported by mineral spines. The sail can flush copper, violet, or warning orange, and it serves both as a radiator and as a display organ.

It communicates through slow pulses of light along its flanks, through low rumbling calls that vibrate through the ground, and through clicks that echo off glass-fern trunks. A calm Vaelith glows a steady blue. A curious one ripples with gold. A threatened one flashes red-orange and lifts its plates, making itself look suddenly larger and spiny.

When threatened, the Vaelith inflates throat sacs, flares its plates, and sprays a caustic mist from glands near its tail. The mist smells sharply of ozone and burned sugar. Its main predator is the Ghar, a blind pack hunter that tracks by vibration. A Vaelith escapes by leaping into the glass-fern canopy, where its hooks and grasping arms let it climb with startling speed.

Ossmora is a slow-rotating super-Earth orbiting an orange dwarf star. Its terminator zone—the narrow band between eternal day and eternal night—is a warm, humid labyrinth of black mudflats, shallow brackish seas, and forests of glass-reed. The air is thick, about 1.4 times Earth pressure, heavy with carbon dioxide and the faint sting of sulfur. Gravity is 1.3g. In this amber twilight lives the Yara: a six-limbed amphibious omnivore humans have nicknamed the “mire-sphinx.”

An adult Yara is roughly 2.3 meters from snout to tail, stands about 1.1 meters at the shoulder, and weighs between 160 and 220 kilograms. Its body is long and low, like a salamander crossed with an otter. Overlapping ceramic-like scales cover its back and flanks, colored a deep indigo that shifts to muddy brown when it buries itself in silt. The belly is pale, mottled with faint violet. A translucent dorsal sail runs from the base of its skull to the middle of its tail, supported by thin bony spines. Folded flat, it looks like a ridge of wet glass; raised, it becomes a shimmering fin.

The head is wedge-shaped, with a flexible neck and four eyes. Two large forward-facing eyes have vertical slit pupils and are adapted for dim light. Above them sit two smaller dorsal eyes that detect ultraviolet and polarized light, helping the Yara navigate beneath Ossmora’s heavy cloud layer. Behind each eye is a tympanic membrane for hearing. Around its mouth writhe a dozen chemosensory tendrils, constantly tasting the water and air. Its upper jaw ends in a hard keratinous beak for cracking shells; the lower jaw holds grinding plates. When threatened, it can inflate a throat sac and emit a booming infrasound note that humans feel in their sternum rather than hear.

It has six limbs. The front pair are powerful and webbed, with three hooked claws for digging burrows and climbing glass-reed trunks. The middle pair are shorter and more delicate, used for grooming, handling food, and carrying eggs. The hind pair are long, muscular, and frog-like, allowing sudden leaps across mud channels. The tail is flattened into an oar and edged with thin spines that can erect to sense vibrations or flush pink during displays. In water, the Yara folds its legs and swims with serpentine undulations; on land, it ambles on all six limbs, then bounds when alarmed.

Its skin secretes a slime layer that smells faintly of wet copper and ozone. The slime is antimicrobial and mildly caustic to predators. Along its dorsal sail and flanks run channels of symbiotic bioluminescent bacteria. The Yara can pulse these channels in blue-green waves, creating patterns unique to each individual—a kind of living signature. Under the skin, chromatophores let it flush from indigo to iridescent violet or fade to near-invisibility against the mud.

Internally, the Yara is a study in dual adaptation. It breathes with lungs on land and with vascular gill filaments along its neck and tail base underwater. Its blood is blue-green, using hemocyanin instead of hemoglobin. A large liver-like organ detoxifies sulfur compounds from its prey and environment. A secondary ganglion near the pelvis controls the limbs autonomously, allowing the creature to keep walking or swimming while its main brain sleeps. Sensory pits along its jaw detect the weak electrical fields of hidden prey, and a lateral-line system along its flanks picks up pressure waves.

The Yara is an opportunistic omnivore and scavenger. It eats armored reed-fish, shelled mollusks, fungal fruits, carrion, and mineral-rich clay. Its gut hosts symbiotic bacteria that digest chitin and tough plant matter. It is mostly crepuscular and solitary, digging burrows into mudbanks and lining them with chewed reeds. It marks territory with scent and brief bioluminescent flashes. During storm season, many Yara gather at shallow “singing pools,” where they communicate through light pulses, infrasound rumbles, and tail slaps against the water. Mating pairs align their dorsal sails and pulse in slow duets.

Yara are sequential hermaphrodites. A mature individual lays three to five leathery eggs in a communal mud nest guarded by non-breeding adults. The larvae are aquatic, tadpole-like, with external gills. After about two years they metamorphose into air-breathing juveniles. They reach maturity at eight years and can live up to sixty Earth years.

As a keystone species, the Yara aerates the mud with its digging, spreads fungal spores on its scales, and controls populations of reed-fish and mollusks. It is preyed upon by giant sky-eels and storm-herons, and it tolerates spore-moths that drink its eye secretions and eat parasites from its hide. To a human observer, the Yara looks like a cross between a salamander, an otter, and a living lantern—a creature perfectly built for the amber half-light of a world that never quite sees noon.
